source.title: Why Is Prompt Tuning for Vision-Language Models Robust to Noisy Labels?
source.authors: Cheng-En Wu; Yu Tian; Hai-Chao Yu; Heng Wang; Pedro Morgado; Yu-Hen Hu; Lin-Jie Yang

record.file_problem: Whole paper text supplied, including extended results and appendices; some figures are flattened into text, but key tables are intact.
record.tranche_reason: The study directly tests label-noise robustness in CLIP prompt tuning, but its findings qualify the broader claim: it updates a small shared prompt over a frozen pretrained vision-language model, and reports accuracy under partial noise rather than fitting fully random labels or measuring training error.
record.gate_note: The paper tests CLIP prompt tuning on few-shot image classification with 12.5%, 25%, and 50% noisy training labels, and measures classification accuracy and noisy-to-clean gradient ratios. The cited Zhang et al. finding that DNNs overfit noisy labels is prior work, not a result of this study. No results cover completely random labels, zero training error, test error at chance, random or shuffled inputs, or the claim's regularization comparison in its stated form.
record.test_reason: The paper cites random-label overfitting as background but studies robustness of few-shot CLIP adaptation. Its own results measure held-out accuracy under partial label corruption and noisy-to-clean gradient ratios, without measuring memorization or training-set fit. These do not test V4's joint claim of perfect training fit and degrading generalization, or any other version.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is broadly accurate. The authors attribute prompt tuning's noise robustness to fixed classname tokens and the structure supplied by pretrained CLIP embeddings, supported by ablations and lower noisy-to-clean gradient ratios. Robust losses further improve transfer performance, and the authors use these findings to motivate unsupervised prompt tuning. Their experiments do not establish whether corrupted training labels are memorized.
record.recipe_differences: The intervention is few-shot adaptation of a pretrained CLIP vision-language model by tuning 16 shared prompt tokens, not training a standard deep network from scratch on fully random labels. The study varies partial label noise and evaluates transfer accuracy.
record.method_sensitivity: Dataset, image encoder (ResNet-50 or ViT-B/32), prompt context length, noise type (random or confusion), and loss (cross-entropy or robust loss) affect outcomes. Figure 5 says the optimal context length is dataset dependent; confusion noise causes larger degradation than random noise.

fits_no_version.finding: With frozen CLIP encoders and shared prompt tuning, transfer accuracy decreases as random corruption increases from 0% to 50%; no training-fit measurements accompany these results.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Few-shot CLIP prompt tuning retains substantial held-out classification accuracy under partial random label noise.

fits_no_version.finding: At 50% noise, prompt tuning has lower noisy-to-clean gradient norm ratios than linear probing.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Shared prompt tuning reduces the relative gradient influence of noisy samples compared with linear probing.

fits_no_version.finding: At 50% corruption, confusion noise yields lower prompt-tuning transfer accuracy than uniform random noise on the four recorded datasets.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The robustness of CLIP prompt tuning depends on the structure of label noise.

record.peer_reviewed: IEEE International Conference on Computer Vision (ICCV), 2023
record.problems: The core analysis uses 16-shot classification and only tests noise rates up to 50%; it reports transfer accuracy, not training error. The gradient-ratio results are only described qualitatively in the text and shown in figures. Main experimental accuracy tables do not report uncertainty, though Table 4 reports mean ± standard deviation.
record.rows_left_out: Rows for the remaining datasets and methods in Tables 1–3 were not extracted to keep the catalog under 60 rows while prioritizing multiple noise conditions, gradient results, backbone comparison, and noise-type changes. Figure 1, Figure 2, Figure 5, Figures 8–9 and Table 5 report additional method comparisons or conditions; Figure 1/2/5/8/9 values are figure-only and were not added where they duplicate conditions, while Table 5 is unsupervised pseudo-label tuning rather than the claim's supervised random-label condition.

untested.parts: Fitting completely random labels to near-zero training error, chance test performance, and unchanged architecture and hyperparameters.
Time to fit true versus random labels and convergence slowing with increasing corruption.
Zero-error fitting of shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, and Gaussian-noise inputs.
Perfect training-set fit across corruption levels while test error approaches chance. Partial-noise transfer accuracy alone does not establish this behavior.
Effects of weight decay, dropout, and augmentation on random-label fitting and of their removal on clean-label generalization.
Learning shared real-data patterns before memorizing noisy labels; no separate learning trajectories establish this ordering.

record.verdict_notes: Remove all three V4 limits_scope verdicts: unmeasured training fit is an untested component, and declining transfer accuracy is compatible with V4 rather than a limitation of it. Recorded table values match the supplied text. The 63M figure describes the frozen text encoder, not the number of trained prompt parameters.

versions.untested_parts: No complete random labeling, zero or near-zero training error, test error at chance, or unchanged standard network architecture/training comparison.
No comparison of training time to fit true versus random labels, nor a sweep of corruption fractions from none to all.
No shuffled, independently permuted, or Gaussian-noise inputs.

Evaluates 0%, 12.5%, 25%, and 50% noise rather than a sweep through all noise fractions; reports transfer/test accuracy, not training-set fit error; tests CLIP prompt tuning rather than the same standard deep networks in the claim.
Does not test weight decay, dropout, or data augmentation against random-label fitting or assess their removal's effect on clean-label generalization.
Does not track whether real-label patterns are learned before noisy or random labels over training.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: CLIP prompt tuning on four datasets with 0%, 12.5%, 25%, and 50% random label noise
reader_labels.reason: Transfer accuracy generally decreases as corruption rises, and the study does not measure perfect training-set fit or cover corruption through all labels (R1–R16).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: RN50-PT and ViT-B/32-PT on OxfordPets; 0% to 50% random noise
reader_labels.reason: Both backbones retain substantial transfer accuracy at 50% noise, but accuracy still falls from the clean condition (R21–R28).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: 50% random versus confusion noise on OxfordPets, Food101, DTD, and UCF101
reader_labels.reason: Prompt tuning remains comparatively robust, while the harder confusion-noise condition yields lower accuracy for each dataset in Table 4 (R29–R36).
